item.title: The Land of the Standing-Up Rocks
item.description: A national monument since the 1920s, Chiricahua is America’s newest national park.

item.title: A simple daily fiber supplement reduced arthritis pain and improved strength
item.description: A new clinical trial suggests that a simple daily fiber supplement could significantly reduce knee osteoarthritis pain, improve muscle strength, and make the body less sensitive to pain. Researchers discovered that the benefits may be linked to changes in gut bacteria and the hormone GLP-1, revealing a promising new approach to arthritis relief.

item.title: The autistic brain processes faces differently than scientists thought
item.description: A major new study reveals that autistic children’s brains process faces differently, and those differences may begin earlier than scientists previously thought. Researchers found that brain signals associated with recognizing faces become more specialized as neurotypical children grow older, but show much less change in autistic children. The discovery could help explain why some autistic people have difficulty recognizing faces and reading emotions.

item.title: The asteroid that killed the dinosaurs may have helped ants conquer the world
item.description: The asteroid that killed the dinosaurs may have set the stage for ants to conquer the planet, with a surprising boost from “jumping genes” hidden in their DNA. Scientists discovered that bursts of activity from these mobile genetic elements coincided with the rise of major ant groups and may have helped sharpen their extraordinary ability to communicate through smell.

item.title: Scientists discover the immune system’s hidden sense of touch
item.description: Scientists at McGill University have discovered a surprising new ability of immune cells that could change how we understand long-term immunity. Researchers found that T cells can actually sense how stiff their surrounding tissues are, using these physical signals to help determine whether they develop into long-lasting memory cells that protect against future infections.

item.title: NASA Invites Media to Crew Completion of Yearlong Mars Simulation
item.description: The four volunteers who lived and worked in a simulated NASA Mars mission for more than a year will exit their habitat on Saturday, Oct. 31, after 378 days of isolation in a facility at the agency’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. Health and performance data collected from the simulation can help NASA develop methods […]

item.description: A technician inspects the large sunshade of NASA’s Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor mission in this image released on Oct. 26, 2026. The sunshade structure, which stands 20 feet (6 meters) tall and measures 8 feet (2.4 meters) wide at its base, will keep the infrared space telescope cool as it searches for near-Earth asteroids and […]

item.title: The secret to slower aging may be hiding in your gut
item.description: The secret to aging more slowly may be hiding in your gut. Scientists discovered that certain gut bacteria are strongly linked to how quickly the body ages, with microbial differences accounting for about 15% of the variation in biological aging rates. Some bacterial species were associated with slower aging, while others were linked to accelerated aging.

item.title: Low testosterone may make sugar far more harmful to your liver
item.description: Scientists have discovered that low testosterone and a high-fructose diet can work together to worsen fatty liver disease in mice. Unexpectedly, changes in gut bacteria appear to drive this harmful interaction, revealing a potential new target for preventing liver damage.

item.title: Common drugs may help dangerous viruses spread through the body
item.description: A surprising discovery reveals that widely used anti-inflammatory drugs may unintentionally help dangerous viruses spread through the body. Scientists found that JAK inhibitors, prescribed for rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory diseases, can weaken a crucial immune defense against influenza, COVID-19, and other infections. By suppressing genes that normally fight viruses, these medications may leave patients more vulnerable to infection.

item.title: James Webb discovers a scorching lava planet with a “giant sunscreen”
item.description: A scorching lava planet 280 light-years away has surprised astronomers by apparently maintaining a thick atmosphere despite conditions that should have stripped it away billions of years ago. James Webb Space Telescope observations suggest that TOI-561 b reflects about 75% of incoming starlight, possibly because of mineral clouds that act like a giant sunscreen. The planet may also be continually replenishing its atmosphere through gases released from a global ocean of molten rock.

item.title: Smithsonian scientists just recreated the first 2 billion years of the Universe
item.description: Scientists have created one of the largest and most detailed simulations of the early universe ever made, offering an extraordinary new glimpse into the cosmos shortly after the Big Bang. Called Lumina, the groundbreaking simulation recreates the universe’s first 2 billion years, showing how dark matter, gas, and radiation interacted to give rise to the earliest stars, galaxies, and black holes.

item.title: A tiny laser beam could make computer memory 1,000 times faster
item.description: Scientists at UC San Diego have developed a surprising new way to store digital information using light instead of magnets, potentially paving the way for smaller, faster, and more energy-efficient memory devices. By precisely shaping and shrinking an ultrafast laser beam, researchers demonstrated that they could switch magnetic states in a material, the basic process used to write digital data. The technique could potentially operate more than 1,000 times faster than conventional magnetic switching methods.

item.title: How a Johnson Mentor Shapes the Next Generation of NASA Talent
item.description: When Rice University student Malvika Bhardwaj asked her mentor Daniel Cohen, a Guidance, Navigation & Control (GN&C) engineer at NASA’s Johnson Space Center, whether he had time to keep teaching interns with his busy workload, he answered, “You decide what’s important.” In honor of National Mentoring Day on Oct. 27, Bhardwaj reflects on how Cohen’s […]

item.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
item.description: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

item.title: Scientists discover a surprising clue to why some brains resist Alzheimer’s
item.description: Why do some people stay mentally sharp even when their brains show signs of Alzheimer’s disease? Scientists in the Netherlands may have uncovered an important clue hidden in a rare group of immature brain cells. Researchers discovered that these cells remain present even in people over 80, but their behavior differs dramatically between those who develop dementia and those who remain cognitively healthy.

item.title: A-81 Reaches South Georgia
item.description: The Antarctic iceberg made a relatively quick exit from the Weddell Sea, only to slow at the edge of a remote island’s underwater shelf.

item.title: Mayo Clinic discovers new ways to fight the “zombie” cells that drive aging
item.description: Mayo Clinic scientists have uncovered surprising new insights into “zombie cells,” aging cells that linger in the body and contribute to inflammation and disease. Seven studies reveal why these cells are harmful and identify new strategies for targeting them, including a natural compound found in tomatoes. In aging mice, experimental treatments reduced inflammation and improved physical and brain health. The findings could open the door to therapies that combat some of the biological processes behind aging.

item.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
item.description: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.

item.title: The surprisingly simple exercise that could lower your blood pressure
item.description: A surprisingly simple exercise routine could help lower blood pressure without requiring daily workouts or expensive equipment. In a study of 100 adults, researchers found that wall squats performed just once or twice a week helped maintain significant reductions in systolic blood pressure over the short term.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 27 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03390-8 Regulatory pushback stalled the field. But researchers are optimistic about mind-altering drugs as potential treatments for depression and mood disorders.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 27 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03461-w A failed rescue mission means that the Swift observatory will fall into Earth’s atmosphere next week, but it leaves a massive archive of data for scientists to explore.

item.title: Could measuring immune health reshape medical care?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 27 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03396-2 Finding practical ways to analyse the state of a person’s immune system could guide treatment decisions and create opportunities for disease prevention.

item.title: Mysterious flickering brain signals could help to unlock secrets of consciousness
item.description: Nature, Published online: 27 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03384-6 Monkeys’ brain activity flips 15 times per second between patterns linked to objects of which the monkeys are aware and patterns for objects outside their awareness.

item.title: Global climate body fights for survival: why the IPCC must be saved
item.description: Nature, Published online: 27 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03403-6 The UN organization faces perhaps the most serious crisis in its nearly 40-year history — but it is too precious to lose.

item.title: Can scientists reliably tell if a novel is written using AI?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 27 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03394-4 Computer scientist Tuhin Chakrabarty talks about detecting AI-generated prose — and why it matters.

item.title: Scientists solve a 30-year mystery behind inflammatory bowel disease
item.description: Scientists have identified a hidden cause of inflammatory bowel disease: antibodies that disable the immune system’s natural ability to control inflammation, potentially explaining severe illness in thousands of patients. The breakthrough also solves a 30-year genetic mystery and could pave the way for more precise diagnoses and targeted treatments.

While it is a wind-swept dusty vista today, billions of years ago it was home to a river channel that fed fresh water into […]

item.title: NASA’s Perseverance Offers Clues to Protect Crews From Mars Dust
item.description: Over 1,645 Martian days, NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover measured the fine and ultrafine Martian dust particles found clinging to samples of spacesuit materials that are carried aboard the rover, including some that are small enough to penetrate the lungs and enter the bloodstream. The findings will be published Tuesday, Oct. 27, in the Proceedings of […]

item.title: Exercise doesn't just strengthen your heart. It rewires it
item.description: Regular exercise does more than strengthen the heart. New research reveals that it actually reshapes the nerves controlling how the heart functions, and the changes are surprisingly different on the left and right sides of the body.

item.title: A 2,700-year-old solar eclipse just revealed something surprising about Earth
item.description: A solar eclipse recorded more than 2,700 years ago is revealing surprising secrets about Earth's rotation and the Sun's ancient behavior. By correcting an eight-kilometer error in the location of an ancient Chinese capital, scientists were able to reconstruct a total solar eclipse that occurred in 709 BCE and obtain more accurate measurements of how fast Earth was spinning at the time.

item.title: Chinese scientists discover “D-rex,” a giant fungus with roots stretching back 65 million years
item.description: Scientists have discovered a giant new fungus in China that grows up to 20 inches tall and weighs nearly five pounds, making it the largest known of its kind. Dubbed “D-rex,” its evolutionary lineage appears to have emerged shortly after the dinosaurs went extinct, raising intriguing questions about how that ancient catastrophe may have shaped its evolution.

item.title: New 3D thermal invisibility cloak makes objects disappear from infrared cameras
item.description: Researchers have developed a groundbreaking 3D invisibility cloak that can hide complex objects from infrared cameras while protecting them from extreme heat and cold. Instead of blocking heat, the device guides it around an object, making the object appear invisible to thermal imaging from virtually any direction. Successfully built and tested, the cloak could transform electronics cooling, thermal protection, and stealth technology.

item.title: Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain
item.description: Scientists have filmed tiny magnetic vortices called skyrmions melting out of an organized lattice for the first time, revealing new ways to manipulate these unusual structures. The breakthrough could help make brain-like computers a reality, potentially enabling dramatically smaller and more energy-efficient technology.

item.title: Archaeologists may have just found the world's oldest shipwreck
item.description: A mysterious shipwreck off Turkey’s coast may be the oldest ever discovered, dating back approximately 4,500 years to the age of the Egyptian pyramids. Although the wooden vessel has disappeared, its surviving pottery cargo reveals clues about an ancient trading network that may have connected distant Mediterranean civilizations. Researchers believe the ship may have crashed against rocks during a storm while transporting valuable goods such as oil, wine, or tree resin.

item.title: AI detects “invisible” signs of pancreatic cancer years before diagnosis
item.description: A powerful new AI system could help doctors detect pancreatic cancer years before it becomes visible on conventional scans. The technology, called REDMOD, identified hidden warning signs an average of 475 days before diagnosis and was nearly twice as sensitive as experienced radiologists. By spotting cancer-related changes at their earliest stages, it could dramatically improve the chances of successful treatment for one of the deadliest forms of cancer.

item.title: Scientists discover Arctic sea ice loss could be far worse than predicted
item.description: Arctic winter sea ice could disappear much faster than scientists previously expected, according to new research using climate clues from 6,000 years ago. By comparing ancient ocean sediments with modern climate models, researchers found that future winter ice coverage may be roughly one million square kilometers smaller than earlier predictions suggested.

item.title: A simple liquid can stop cavities without drilling, major study confirms
item.description: A simple liquid painted onto teeth in seconds can stop cavities without drilling, injections, or anesthesia, according to a major clinical trial involving young children. The inexpensive treatment could spare thousands of children painful dental procedures and surgery while paving the way for broader FDA-approved use.

item.title: Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers
item.description: Scientists have discovered a way to operate multiple silicon qubits simultaneously with remarkable accuracy, overcoming a major challenge in scaling up quantum computers. Their new technique maintained accuracy of approximately 99.9% even when all five qubits were running at once, opening the door to larger and more powerful quantum processors.

item.title: Nerve activity initiates autoimmune hair loss
item.description: Nature, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03258-x Understanding the triggers of autoimmunity might lead to better therapies, with hair loss among the conditions for which underpinning factors have come to light.

item.title: Women might have invented language — but not alone
item.description: Nature, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03392-6 An eloquent analysis of the origins of human speech suggests that social cohesion, not conflict, drove our use of words.

item.title: Daily briefing: The Selfish Gene, 50 years on
item.description: Nature, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03463-8 What biologists think of Dawkins’s big idea now. Plus. how the subject of a new film haunts science and a bacterium that makes its own MOFs.

item.title: Are salaries getting worse? Many scientists think so
item.description: Nature, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03398-0 Nature’s survey of almost 4,000 researchers shows that you’re not alone if you struggle to make ends meet or your last pay rise is a distant memory.

item.title: Can science make your dog live longer? Longevity craze comes to pets
item.description: Nature, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03447-8 The emerging science — and industry — of animal longevity is attracting interest from companies and academics alike.

item.title: Glimpsing archaeal microbes on the move
item.description: Nature, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03259-w How and when did cells gain the ability to crawl? Live imaging of cells from close relatives of early eukaryotes fills in a major gap in the understanding of cellular evolution.

item.title: Evolutionary ‘game-changer’: weird armoured amphibian lived in ancient seas
item.description: Nature, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03440-1 The creature’s armour cladding probably enabled it to tolerate the salty seas of the Late Triassic.

item.title: The Selfish Gene, 50 years on — it’s time for an update
item.description: Nature, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03393-5 A focus on the gene alone has become outdated. Books that capture the complexity of life deserve centre stage.

item.title: Mentoring a lab colleague? Share your ‘CV of failures’ with them
item.description: Nature, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03410-7 Melanie Stefan became a ‘poster child of failure’ after writing an article about it. Now she urges senior colleagues to be more open about career setbacks.

item.title: Brazil election: many scientists relieved as Lula wins surprise victory
item.description: Nature, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03446-9 Scientific organizations in Brazil had rallied around the incumbent president, who defied expectations to defeat his opponent in a run-off.

item.title: Scientists reveal the hidden danger of missing blood pressure medication
item.description: Missing blood pressure medication could mean losing much of its protection against heart attacks and strokes, according to an analysis of more than 91,000 people. Patients who consistently took their medication experienced an 11% reduction in major cardiovascular events, while those who missed too many doses saw little or no measurable benefit.

item.title: Just two drinks a day may be far riskier than you think
item.description: A major new study reveals that drinking just two alcoholic beverages a day is associated with a 1 in 25 lifetime risk of death from alcohol-related causes, challenging the idea that moderate drinking is harmless. Researchers also found no significant overall health benefits from alcohol, with risks rising as consumption increases.

item.title: Three giant black holes discovered in a galaxy from the dawn of time
item.description: Astronomers have discovered three actively feeding black holes inside a single galaxy more than 12.5 billion light-years away, revealing a remarkable scene from the universe’s infancy. Two of the black holes are separated by just 620 light-years and are expected to eventually merge, while a third lurks farther away. One weighs an astonishing 80 million suns, and another is growing faster than conventional theories predict.

item.title: New evidence suggests spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater
item.description: Millions of years after animals first conquered land, some took an extraordinary evolutionary U-turn and returned to the water. Using machine learning and thousands of fossil measurements, Yale scientists have uncovered surprising clues about which prehistoric creatures truly became aquatic. Their findings suggest that Spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater, while some ancient marine reptiles previously thought to be fully aquatic actually spent considerable time on land.

item.title: Scientists discover how pancreatic cancer rewrites its DNA to escape treatment
item.description: Scientists have discovered how pancreatic cancer cells continually reshape their genetic makeup to become more aggressive, spread, and evade treatment. In laboratory experiments, blocking a key gene reversed some of these dangerous changes, revealing a potential new way to fight the deadly disease.

item.title: Low-dose aspirin linked to 70% lower dementia risk, but there's a catch
item.description: A common, inexpensive medication could hold an unexpected clue to preventing dementia. Researchers found that older adults with a specific genetic profile had a 70% lower relative risk of dementia when taking low-dose aspirin, even though previous studies found no overall protective effect. The discovery suggests that genetics could help explain why some people benefit while others do not.

item.title: This mysterious mushroom makes people see hundreds of tiny humans
item.description: For nearly a century, people in distant parts of the world have reported a bizarre experience after eating certain wild mushrooms: seeing dozens or even hundreds of tiny, colorful humans moving through the real world. Now, scientists have identified a mushroom species, Lanmaoa asiatica, responsible for these extraordinary hallucinations in China and the Philippines.

item.title: Popular cannabis sleep gummies may have a hidden dark side
item.description: A cannabis-derived ingredient commonly found in sleep gummies may be more habit-forming than previously thought, with new research showing that repeated exposure caused tolerance and withdrawal symptoms in mice. Scientists warn that CBN may carry risks similar to THC, although its long-term effects in humans remain largely unknown.

item.title: Astronomers may have discovered the first moon beyond our Solar System
item.description: Astronomers have uncovered evidence of a bizarre, potentially historic discovery: the first moon ever detected beyond our Solar System. Unlike familiar moons, this mysterious object is at least as massive as Jupiter and orbits a brown dwarf, which itself circles a star. The unusual arrangement challenges traditional definitions of planets and moons, leaving scientists unsure what to call it.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden flaw that challenges 40 years of superconductor science
item.description: A superconducting material studied for 40 years has turned out to be far more complex than scientists believed. Advanced 3D imaging revealed a hidden patchwork of crystal structures, with unusually wide boundaries that may weaken superconductivity. The discovery challenges decades of scientific assumptions and could explain why some superconductors outperform others.

item.title: Mediterranean diet may boost tiny proteins that protect the heart and brain
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a surprising new clue to why the Mediterranean diet is so good for the heart, brain, and healthy aging. Researchers at USC found that older adults who closely followed the diet had higher levels of two tiny proteins, humanin and SHMOOSE, produced by the mitochondria, the energy-producing structures inside cells. These proteins have been linked to protection against heart disease, Alzheimer's disease, and age-related damage.

item.title: ctDNA clearance and outcomes for resectable lung cancer from NeoCOAST-2
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11328-3 ctDNA clearance and outcomes for resectable lung cancer from NeoCOAST-2

item.title: Could lowering high blood pressure be as simple as stimulating your ear?
item.description: A small device that gently stimulates nerves through the ear could offer a new way to tackle stubborn high blood pressure. In a clinical trial of 63 patients already taking medication, the treatment proved safe, easy to use at home, and well tolerated. Although it did not significantly outperform a placebo overall, patients with more severe hypertension showed promising reductions in blood pressure.

item.title: A hidden bias in human language challenges 70 years of science
item.description: A groundbreaking study challenges 70 years of assumptions about how human language works. By analyzing billions of word uses, scientists discovered that meaning is organized around power, danger, and order rather than emotion alone. Even more surprisingly, human language shows a powerful hidden preference for safety, suggesting that our words may reflect ancient survival instincts.

item.title: NASA’s asteroid Bennu samples reveal a 4.5-billion-year-old secret
item.description: Tiny samples from asteroid Bennu are rewriting scientists' understanding of how our Solar System formed. New evidence suggests that Bennu was born where material from the inner and outer Solar System mixed, with Jupiter playing a surprising role in shaping its formation.

item.title: Astronomers uncover a mysterious magnetic web above the Sun
item.description: The Sun’s seemingly peaceful regions are hiding a surprisingly complex magnetic world. Using a balloon-borne telescope high above Earth, scientists discovered delicate, thread-like magnetic structures woven through the solar atmosphere, apparently shaped by twisting motions on the Sun’s surface. They also mapped magnetic fields inside towering jets of solar material, revealing how those fields change with height.

item.title: These tiny snakes roll four times faster than they slither
item.description: Tiny snakes in Southeast Asia have mastered an extraordinary escape technique: rolling across the ground at speeds up to four times faster than ordinary slithering. Scientists discovered that dwarf reedsnakes accomplish this feat through precisely coordinated body movements that allow their bodies to rotate while their heads remain remarkably stable.

item.title: Your blood could reveal inflammatory bowel disease 10 years before diagnosis
item.description: A major study has uncovered hidden warning signs of inflammatory bowel disease in the blood up to 10 years before diagnosis. Researchers discovered distinct antibody patterns that could help predict who would later develop Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis, even distinguishing people at risk of more complicated disease.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden switch that burns fat and blocks new fat cells
item.description: Scientists have discovered that switching off a protein called Mitch makes human cells burn more fat and prevents new fat cells from developing. The breakthrough builds on experiments in mice that showed remarkable resistance to obesity and improved muscular endurance, raising hopes for a new approach to weight-loss treatment.

item.title: This 150-million-year-old bird had dinosaur teeth and a strange secret
item.description: A 150-million-year-old fossil discovered in China reveals a bizarre early bird with sharp teeth, a dinosaur-like claw, and a body built for life on the ground rather than flight. Scientists believe it represents the earliest known example of flight loss in birds, overturning assumptions about how these animals evolved.

item.title: Glioblastoma breakthrough reveals how brain cancer cells become more aggressive
item.description: Scientists discovered that the thick, sticky fluid surrounding glioblastoma tumors can make brain cancer cells smaller, more flexible, and better at invading surrounding tissue. Even more troubling, some of these changes persist after the cells leave the thick fluid, revealing a previously overlooked mechanism that could help this deadly cancer spread.

item.title: One of Earth’s most powerful supervolcanoes is refilling with fresh magma
item.description: Deep beneath Japan’s Kikai caldera, a massive magma reservoir is refilling 7,300 years after one of the most powerful volcanic eruptions in Earth's recent geological history. Scientists used underwater seismic surveys to reveal a vast store of magma that appears to have accumulated since the ancient catastrophe. The discovery could help explain how supervolcanoes like Yellowstone and Toba rebuild their magma supplies.

item.title: Dental implants can hijack your immune system, scientists discover
item.description: Researchers have uncovered a surprising reason dental implant infections often resist antibiotics: the implants themselves can contribute to the problem. Bacteria corrode titanium implants, releasing microscopic particles that hijack immune cells, trigger destructive inflammation, and accelerate jawbone loss.

item.title: Breakthrough PTSD treatment achieves 68% remission rate in clinical trial
item.description: A newly FDA-cleared PTSD treatment uses personalized brain mapping and magnetic stimulation to target abnormal brain activity, with a clinical trial reporting a 52% reduction in symptoms and 68% remission. Researchers believe the technology could transform PTSD care and pave the way for more precise treatments for other mental health conditions.

item.title: MIT scientists build a tiny robot that swims using living muscle cells
item.description: MIT engineers have built a paper-thin swimming robot powered by living muscle cells that respond to flashes of light, allowing it to swim and steer through water. The breakthrough could pave the way for tiny, self-healing biological robots capable of exploring fragile environments that ordinary machines cannot safely navigate.

item.title: A tiny defect in a crystal reveals a big quantum surprise
item.description: Researchers have solved a long-standing challenge in understanding how tiny defects in materials like diamond and silicon carbide behave when exposed to light. Their new computational method revealed a surprisingly important energy-loss mechanism in silicon carbide that scientists had previously underestimated. The finding helps explain a mystery that has puzzled researchers for years and could improve the design of quantum computers and sensors.

item.title: Scientists discover a surprising double benefit of exercise for Parkinson’s
item.description: A seven-year study found that people with Parkinson’s disease who were more physically active experienced slower declines in memory, thinking, and movement abilities. Those exercising more than eight hours per week showed almost no average cognitive decline, suggesting that staying active may offer important benefits as the disease progresses.

item.title: Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has vanished in just five years
item.description: Switzerland’s glaciers are disappearing at an alarming rate, losing more than 5% of their ice volume in 2026 alone. Some of the country’s most famous glaciers experienced their worst melting on record, while several smaller glaciers vanished completely. Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has disappeared in just five years, driven by unusually snowless winters and extreme summer heat.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden messaging system deep inside the brain
item.description: A tiny region deep within the brain has surprised scientists by revealing a remarkably sophisticated communication system. Previously thought to broadcast the same chemical signal throughout the brain, this region actually sends targeted messages that help control learning, attention, and behavior, according to new research in mice.

item.title: Scientists propose a way to detect dangerous “mirror life” before it exists
item.description: Scientists have proposed a way to detect “mirror life,” a hypothetical form of life that could pose serious risks to humans, animals, and ecosystems if artificially created. Using special fluorescent molecules and a type of polarized light also used in 3D movie technology, researchers believe they could distinguish ordinary organisms from their mirror-image counterparts.

item.title: 40 years later, Chernobyl's nuclear fallout is not what scientists expected
item.description: Forty years after the Chornobyl disaster, tiny radioactive particles still linger in the soil, carrying a dangerous legacy. Using powerful X-rays, scientists discovered that some of these particles have remained surprisingly stable, trapping radioactive substances inside instead of releasing them into the environment.

item.title: Nearly 3,000 exploding stars challenge our understanding of the Universe
item.description: A massive analysis of 2,884 exploding stars has uncovered new evidence that dark energy, the mysterious force accelerating the universe’s expansion, may change over time. The findings challenge a cornerstone of modern cosmology and could reshape our understanding of how the universe works.

item.title: Cambridge scientists create a $10 chip that could put a medical lab on your wrist
item.description: Cambridge researchers have created a groundbreaking $10 optical sensor that delivers the precision of laboratory equipment in a device small enough for wearable technology. It identified foods, plastics, and medicines with 100% accuracy in tests and demonstrated the ability to monitor blood glucose, alcohol, and other health markers without invasive procedures.

item.title: Author Correction: DYNLL1 binds to MRE11 to limit DNA end resection in BRCA1-deficient cells
item.description: Nature, Published online: 23 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11303-y Author Correction: DYNLL1 binds to MRE11 to limit DNA end resection in BRCA1-deficient cells

item.title: Elusive snow leopards and evasive particles: Books in brief
item.description: Nature, Published online: 23 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03395-3 Andrew Robinson reviews five of the best science picks.

item.title: Sleep declines in rural communities after electricity arrives
item.description: Nature, Published online: 23 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03318-2 Scientists tracked the changing sleep patterns of Indigenous people in Argentina who gained access to mains electricity — and smart phones.

item.title: Briefing Chat: How physicists successfully trapped the electron's antimatter equivalent
item.description: Nature, Published online: 23 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03418-z Nature staff discuss how precisely measuring a positron could shed light on one of physics’ greatest mysteries — plus, the latest on an ambitious mission to a Martian moon.

item.title: First person infected with rare Shamonda virus: what we know
item.description: Nature, Published online: 23 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03416-1 Infectious-disease researchers say the risk of the livestock pathogen moving between people is low.

item.title: Elizabeth Holmes film enthrals — but her legacy haunts science
item.description: Nature, Published online: 23 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03383-7 You Can See Everything brings blood-testing start-ups back into the public eye. They persevere in Theranos’s shadow.

item.title: Moderna mRNA vaccine almost halves the risk of skin cancer returning
item.description: Nature, Published online: 23 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03417-0 Long-awaited results from phase III trial show huge benefits for treatment-resistant melanoma.

item.title: I’m expected to work excessive hours in the lab. Should I speak up about my disability?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 23 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02582-6 What can a researcher in an overworked laboratory do to take care of themselves and their lab-mates, and how should they navigate medical disclosure?

item.title: Birds are more afraid of women than men. Scientists have no idea why
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a strange pattern in urban bird behavior: Across five European countries and 37 species, birds consistently fled sooner when approached by women than men. Researchers have no clear explanation for the difference, raising intriguing questions about how birds recognize and respond to humans.

item.title: Oxford scientists discover how viruses build themselves without a blueprint
item.description: Scientists have captured virus-like particles assembling themselves step by step, revealing how a surprisingly simple process of trial and error produces complex structures with remarkable precision. The discovery uncovers a crucial molecular turning point that speeds up assembly and could lead to new ways to disrupt viruses and develop vaccines.

item.title: Can a 'lullaby' save coral reefs from extinction?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 22 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03414-3 From underwater speakers to growing super-corals, scientists battle to save reefs around the world.

item.title: A first for CRISPR: powerful prime editing alters DNA directly in the human body
item.description: Nature, Published online: 22 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03371-x Application of the high-precision technique is part of a clinical trial to treat a genetic disease that can cause liver and nerve damage.

item.title: Teen depression and anxiety predicted by childhood brain development
item.description: Nature, Published online: 22 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03357-9 Analysis of nearly 30,000 brain scans yields detailed timeline of how the brain matures — and hints at the consequences of disrupting it.

item.title: Can maths survive AI? Fields medallist Terence Tao calls for a ‘Maths 2.0’ world
item.description: Nature, Published online: 22 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03389-1 As machines race ahead in solving problems, mathematicians must establish a new era that prizes human understanding over simply publishing more solutions.

item.title: Daily briefing: The tell-tale features of a Denisovan
item.description: Nature, Published online: 22 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03438-9 See what gave Denisovans their distinct look. Plus, a vaccine trial for Ebola could kick off this week in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and what makes a great climate graphic.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03376-6 Experiment shows how these ecosystems could protect coastlines from huge storms — plus, new evidence hints at what Denisovans might have looked like.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11252-6 Author Correction: Catalyst-free, microdroplet-mediated waste plastic conversion to diacids

item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03320-8 Large language models suggest more tests, referrals and medications than human physicians do, driving up the cost of care.

item.title: Surprise! White dwarf stars come in a rainbow of colours
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03319-1 Analysis of some nearby stars shows that, despite their name, these bodies can be pink, yellow and more.

item.title: To heal sick cities, scientists and residents must work together
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03161-5 Tolullah Oni has developed a platform to transfer the intellectual capital of African diaspora scholars back to the continent.

item.title: An AI tool improves weather forecasts up to a month ahead
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03077-0 An innovative artificial-intelligence application enhances weather forecasting in the difficult subseasonal range, providing accurate forecasts of precipitation, temperature and pressure 3–5 weeks in advance. The tool refines both physics- and AI-based weather models and improves the early prediction of extremes of heat, cold, rainfall and flooding.

item.title: Using AI to offer personalized health advice
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03065-4 The use of artificial-intelligence tools in medicine is increasing. What types of technology might be on the horizon and how can such health-advice tools be tested?

item.title: Global emissions slow — but world hurtles towards 2 °C of warming
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03355-x The United Nations’ latest climate report is a stark reminder that limiting warming to the safest levels is now likely to be out of reach.

item.title: Huge mapping study reveals how your brain tracks what your body is feeling
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03334-2 Signals in the insula region, deep in the brain, can make people feel hot, tingly and nauseous.

item.title: Plastics embedded with enzymes degrade readily in the sea
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03282-x Embedding enzymes that break down ester bonds into compostable polyesters enables rapid and complete biodegradation even in microbe-scarce environments. This method is effective in marine sites ranging from coastal sea water to the deep sea, and could therefore contribute towards solving the global plastic pollution problem.

item.title: The Bursar
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03110-2 A good way to learn?

item.title: This is what the mysterious Denisovans looked like
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03360-0 Archaeologists identified skull fragments from China as belonging to this group of ancient human relatives.

item.title: Can plants defend coasts against storms?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03063-6 Salt-marsh plants can protect inland areas against huge waves — but seemingly only up to a point, and big storms cause progressive damage.

item.title: Worms live longer in cool conditions thanks to a muscle-derived molecule
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03066-3 In nematodes, a metabolite induced by the cold links low temperatures to a body-wide signal that promotes longevity. This signalling system is also seen in human cells.

item.title: Daily briefing: How tech billionaires are changing science funding
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03400-9 Ultra-rich philanthropists are disrupting biomedical science. Plus, why physicists have kept an antimatter particle caged for months and whether it’s really possible to be swallowed by a whale and survive.

item.title: Cave stalagmites document global patterns in monsoon rainfall over the past 450,000 years
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03285-8 A 450,000-year stalagmite record of rainfall in the Amazon Basin , combined with existing Asian records, shows that the global monsoon system has oscillated regularly, strengthening in one hemisphere while weakening in the other. However, during intervals of warmth and warming climate, monsoons in both hemispheres failed for millennia.

item.title: Large-scale single crystals printed layer by layer
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03257-y A 3D-printing method has made single crystals of metals and alloys in complex shapes and up to one metre in length, as needed for advanced technological applications.

item.title: A single antimatter particle in a cage opens door to ‘revolutionary’ physics
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03342-2 Physicists trap and cool down positron for months to measure its ‘magnetic moment’ with extraordinary precision.

item.title: Robert Williamson obituary: geneticist who mapped genes for muscular dystrophy and cystic fibrosis
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03375-7 Researcher and policy adviser who championed tests and treatments for genetic diseases.

item.title: Fabric user interface can be worn on your sleeve — and machine-washed
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03064-5 Touch-sensitive, light-emitting yarn can turn everyday clothing into washable, bendable user interfaces with dynamic graphics and versatile computing functions.

item.title: How tech billionaires are disrupting biomedical science
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03311-9 Money from the world’s increasingly prosperous technology entrepreneurs has been flooding into biomedical research. Is it changing how science is done?

item.title: How a new wave of science philanthropists can have the greatest impact
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03326-2 Tech entrepreneurs are bringing an engineer’s eye to research funding. They must be open about their findings to reap maximum benefit.

item.title: Multimodal precision diagnostics in clinical xenotransplantation
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11096-0 Now that hyperacute rejection of pig xenografts can be reliably prevented, subtler immune-mediated graft injuries have emerged that conventional diagnostics often miss; a multimodal precision diagnostic framework is proposed to detect these injuries earlier, guide personalized immunosuppression and inform future gene editing strategies.

item.title: The contribution of salt marshes to wave attenuation during extreme storms
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11145-8 Salt marsh platforms resist erosion under extreme waves, but vegetation damage reduces wave attenuation; substantial wave attenuation by vegetation is mainly limited to low-energy marsh coasts with waves below 1 m.

item.title: Zeolite-catalysed olefin carbonylation based on tuning spatial confinement
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11183-2 The use of zeolites with an appropriate pore structure combined with a high CO/olefin ratio is shown to catalyse olefin carbonylation and produce primary and secondary carboxylic acids as the main products.

item.title: Cold activates a BH2 metabolic network promoting longevity and proteostasis
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11152-9 A multi-tissue signalling system links cold temperature to enhanced longevity and proteostasis in Caenorhabditis elegans.

item.title: WEE1 opposes APC/C<sup>CDH1</sup> activity to promote S phase entry
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11188-x Experimental and modelling data indicate that WEE1 promotes re-entry of quiescent cells into the cell cycle, potentially explaining the toxic side effects of WEE1 inhibitors in cancer therapies.

item.title: A single archaeon couples long-chain fatty acid oxidation to methanogenesis
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11207-x Methanoglobus dolicholipophagus AA-75 is a thermophilic archaeon isolated from a Chinese petroleum reservoir that converts methanol into methane, carbon dioxide and acetate, and uses saturated and unsaturated fatty acids to produce methane.

item.title: An environmentally regulated dichotomy in cell lineages of the root
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11179-y An environment-regulated state is identified across multiple cell types at the root tip, revealing a shared dichotomy between cells with and without this state.

item.title: CD51 delineates functionally distinct astrocyte subtypes in neural circuits
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11186-z CD51+ astrocytes promote synapse formation in the developing cortex, circuit plasticity in the hippocampus and circuit remodelling after stroke.

item.title: Persistent neuronal stress signalling underlies Angelman syndrome phenotypes
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11165-4 Genetic and proteomic analyses in human neurons and mouse models of Angelman syndrome (AS) show that loss of the ubiquitin ligase UBE3A leads to an overabundance of asparagine synthetase, and that this is linked with many AS phenotypes.

item.title: Structural basis for protocadherin-1 recognition by New World hantaviruses
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11184-1 The structure of PCDH1 bound to the ANDV spike defines the structural determinants of hantavirus–receptor recognition.
